items.abstract: The usage of the development of machine learning is extremely important these days, especially in power systems. Artificial neural networks (ANN) have been developed and implemented successfully to improve power system performance and solve complex problems. This paper introduces a new machine learning-based approach to the power flow operation using different types of ANNs, including simple feedforward neural networks (SFNN), learning neural networks (TLNN), simple deep neural networks (SDNN), deep feedforward neural networks (DFFNN) and long short long memory neural network (LSTM). The modeling aims to predict the optimal power flow parameters to ensure efficient and economical power system operation considering the power system stability constraints such as voltage control limits and power angle limits. ANN performance is evaluated using each parameter's mean square error (MSE). The study results show high system stability prediction data accuracy, essential for power system operation. The results also confirm that the proposed approach can offer a significant advancement in utilizing machine learning to improve the monitoring of optimal power flow in real-time operation, considering stability constraints.
title: Artificial Neural Network for Stability-Constrained Optimal Power Flow

items.abstract: Undifferentiated pleomorphic/undifferentiated sarcoma frequently exhibits a copy-number-dominant, structurally complex genome in which alteration-centric interpretation can produce a large but poorly discriminated set of candidate drivers. We evaluated whether a constraint-preserving causal reconstruction could recover biologically useful portions of hidden tumor architecture from an individual observational molecular state and whether the resulting latent state generated mechanistic vulnerability hypotheses that were not reducible to conventional driver matching. Publicly derived TCGA-SARC data for TCGA- QC-A6FX were analyzed using Biology First Intelligence (BFI), a proprietary constraint-preserving causal-reconstruction framework, with explicit separation of measurement, characterization, causal inference, and post-freeze therapeutic interpretation. Two allele-specific copy-number representations converged on pervasive minor-allele loss: 78.22% and 78.20% of autosomal sequence had minor copy number zero, with 99.96% agreement on minor-zero status across overlapping sequence. Approximately 65% of the autosomal genome occupied major-only CN4/3/2 states, while focal/regional amplification reached CN23-24 in a recurrently bounded chr6q interval. Absolute gene-level copy-number scale was materially discordant across processing lineages, preventing point identification of exact ploidy or a discrete whole-genome-doubling event. The surviving model set nevertheless shared an invariant architecture comprising extensive allele-specific structural-genome remodeling, pervasive homolog- specific allelic collapse, survival of a copy-number-elevated aneuploid lineage, and superimposed multi-chromosomal amplification. The reconstruction was therefore classified as partial rather than fully identified. After freezing the causal model, mechanistic analysis yielded state-dependent hypotheses involving mitotic-fidelity machinery, replication-stress tolerance, proteostasis/dosage homeostasis, and retained-homolog dependency discovery. Several of these hypotheses were not naturally recoverable from the alteration-to-target baseline, which instead emphasized amplified loci such as GRM1, CDK6, CCNE1, MCL1, and AURKA. This case demonstrates that BFI can transform a high-dimensional list of genomic consequences into a falsifiable, set-valued latent architecture while preserving non-identification, and can expose state-maintenance hypotheses beyond gene-centric target matching. Biological and therapeutic validity remain untested and require orthogonal structural, temporal, and functional assays. Keywords: Biology First Intelligence; causal reconstruction; undifferentiated sarcoma; copy-number alteration; loss of heterozygosity; aneuploidy; whole- genome doubling; precision oncology; network vulnerability; driver matching CASE RESULT. The analytical problem addressed here is not the detection of genomic abnormalities but the inverse identification of a parsimonious generating architecture from an incomplete endpoint. In TCGA-QC-A6FX, the observable genome contains numerous amplified loci, extensive allelic imbalance, and mutually inconsistent absolute-copy representations. A feature-matching workflow therefore yields many candidate targets but does not specify the disease state that makes the abnormalities coexist. Constraint-preserving reconstruction instead identifies the stable information that survives competing causal histories and measurement disagreement, then derives post-freeze dependencies from that state. The result is a set-valued mechanistic model rather than a single-driver narrative.
title: Constrained Causal Reconstruction of a Single Undifferentiated Sarcoma Reveals a Latent Disease State and Network Vulnerabilities Beyond Driver Matching

items.abstract: <jats:p>The mammalian brain sustains general-purpose cognition on roughly 20 watts, whereas state-ofthe-art artificial neural networks consume many orders of magnitude more energy for narrower competence. We argue that this gap is not incidental but reflects the absence of an explicit thermodynamic objective in standard learning. Here we propose an in silico evolutionary sandbox that subjects spiking graph neural networks (SGNNs) to the same physical pressures that shaped cortex: metabolic maintenance, distance-dependent signaling cost, and wiring volume. Each network is embedded in a three-dimensional Euclidean workspace, computes through leaky integrate-and-fire dynamics with short-term synaptic plasticity, draws energy through a shared astrocyte routing layer rather than isolated reservoirs, and obeys Dale's principle with an evolvable excitatory/inhibitory balance and myelination. Each network is selected by an evolutionary reinforcement loop under a multi-objective fitness function that trades task accuracy against a biophysically itemized metabolic penalty. We formalize the model, specify the multi-scale simulation engine and its structural mutation operators (neurogenesis, synaptogenesis, and activitydependent pruning), and define a pre-registered, falsifiable experimental roadmap. The central, testable predictions are that small-world modularity and heavy-tailed (log-normal) synaptic weights emerge as optimization consequences of thermodynamic constraint, each with an explicit quantitative threshold that would falsify the framework. Implementing the framework and evolving populations under graded energy budgets, we find that metabolic constraint robustly increases network modularity-measured against a degree-preserving null and replicated at N = 120 where edges greatly outnumber nodes (ρ = +0.89, p = 10-4)-while the raw smallworld index is shown to be partly a density artifact. Contrary to prediction, the constraint does not yield log-normal weights (refuted at both scales) or a net efficiency gain. Ablations show the topological effect depends on short-term plasticity and excitatory/inhibitory balance but not on the astrocyte or myelination layers. These are concrete, falsifiable outcomes; the central contribution is an open, reproducible framework that renders such claims quantitatively testable, offering a controllable testbed for evolutionary neurobiology and a design principle for energy-proportional neuromorphic hardware.</jats:p>
title: Mapping the Metabolic Pareto Frontier: An Evolutionary Spiking Graph Neural Network Framework for Studying Energy-Constrained Neural Organization

items.abstract: <jats:p>Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks; however, their deployment on resource-constrained edge devices remains challenging due to high storage and computational requirements. This work proposes a lightweight neural network compression pipeline designed to enable efficient deployment of deep models in constrained environments. The proposed framework integrates knowledge distillation, structured pruning, and dynamic quantization to significantly reduce model size while maintaining competitive predictive performance. Experiments were conducted on the widely used datasets MNIST and Fashion-MNIST to evaluate the effectiveness of the compression strategy. The results demonstrate that the proposed pipeline achieves approximately 20 times model size reduction while preserving classification accuracy with only marginal degradation compared to the original model. items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper proposes a moment-constrained neural-network-based non-oscillatory difference operator for shock capturing in numerical simulations of hyperbolic conservation laws. Built on a finite-difference scheme with a six-point stencil, the method employs a multilayer perceptron to learn nonlinear corrections to local difference coefficients and then enforces low-order discrete moment constraints through a subspace projection step. This design enables adaptive control of numerical dissipation and suppresses spurious oscillations near discontinuities while retaining resolution in smooth regions. Numerical experiments show that the proposed operator effectively preserves profile shapes in linear advection problems and stably captures the main discontinuous structures in the Sod and Lax shock tubes, two-dimensional Riemann problems, the Double Mach Reflection problem, and Rayleigh--Taylor instability. Compared with WENO-Z, the method exhibits lower numerical dissipation while maintaining satisfactory robustness. These results demonstrate that neural networks can serve as nonlinear correction modules within traditional high-order finite-difference schemes. Moreover, the moment constraints offer a practical route toward data-driven shock-capturing schemes that balance accuracy, resolution, and robustness.</jats:p>
title: A Moment-Constrained Neural-Network-Based Shock-Capturing Scheme
